about.title: About me
about.p1: I'm a senior software engineer who loves turning complex problems into simple, reliable products. My favorite work lives at the intersection of design and engineering — interfaces that feel effortless and are built to scale.
about.p2: Over the past eight years I've worked across startups and product studios, leading frontend architecture, building design systems, and shipping features used by millions. I believe the best engineering is invisible: fast, accessible, and dependable.
about.p3: When I'm not coding, you'll find me sketching UI ideas, contributing to open source, or running along the coast with a good podcast.

skillDescriptions.React:
## React

My primary technology for several years. I work with React daily building medium and large-scale production applications.

### What I master
- **Advanced hooks**: `useReducer`, `useContext`, `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, and complex custom hooks.
- **Composition patterns**: render props, compound components, controlled/uncontrolled components.
- **Performance optimization**: `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, code splitting with `Suspense` and `lazy`.
- **Server Components** (React 19) and the new concurrent rendering model.

### Featured projects
I've built real-time analytical dashboards, complete design systems, and e-commerce applications with millions of users, all on React.
skillDescriptions.Nextjs:
## Next.js

Framework of choice for any serious web project. I've been using Next.js since version 12 and have migrated projects through each major version.

### Areas of expertise
- **App Router**: nested layouts, route groups, Server vs Client Components.
- **Rendering strategies**: SSG, SSR, ISR and Partial Pre-rendering (PPR).
- **Built-in optimizations**: `next/image`, `next/font`, metadata API.
- **Middleware** and Edge Runtime for authentication and A/B testing.

### Real experience
From ultra-fast landing pages with 100/100 Lighthouse scores to complex SaaS platforms with authentication, multi-tenancy, and real-time data dashboards.
skillDescriptions.TypeScript:
## TypeScript

I can't imagine starting a new project without TypeScript. I use it in all my projects, both frontend and backend.

### What I bring
- **Advanced typing**: generics, conditional types, mapped types, template literal types.
- **Type inference** that reduces boilerplate without losing safety.
- **Integration** with Zod, tRPC and Prisma for frictionless end-to-end type-safety.
- Strict `tsconfig` configuration tailored to each project.

### Why I value it
TypeScript has saved me countless hours of debugging. Errors appear in the editor, not in production at 3am.
skillDescriptions.TailwindCSS:
## Tailwind CSS

My preferred styling tool. From Tailwind v2 to v4, I've seen the framework evolve and adopted its improvements in each iteration.

### How I use it
- **Custom design tokens** integrated with the project's design system.
- **Variants** with `cva` (class-variance-authority) for polymorphic components.
- **Animations** with `tw-animate-css` and native CSS transitions.
- Automatic bundle optimization: only used classes in production.

### Key advantage
Placing styles alongside markup eliminates context switching and makes code more readable and maintainable.
skillDescriptions.FramerMotion:
## Framer Motion

Library I use to add quality animations to my interfaces without sacrificing performance or accessibility.

### Frequent use cases
- **Smooth page transitions** with layout animations.
- **Micro-interactions**: hover states, press feedback, animated loading skeletons.
- **Scroll-driven animations** with `useScroll` and `useTransform`.
- **Gesture handling** for mobile interfaces (drag, swipe).

### Philosophy
I use animations with intention: they should communicate something, not just decorate. I always respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
skillDescriptions.Accessibility:
## Web Accessibility

Accessibility is not an additional feature, it's part of doing the job right. I have it integrated as part of my development workflow.

### Practices I apply
- **HTML semantics**: I use the correct elements (`button`, `nav`, `main`, `dialog`, etc.).
- **Keyboard**: all interactions are operable without a mouse, with visible focus and logical order.
- **ARIA**: attributes `aria-label`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-live` where semantic HTML is not sufficient.
- **Contrast**: I verify WCAG AA/AAA ratios for text and interactive icons.

### Tools
I use `axe-core`, Lighthouse and screen reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA) to validate.
skillDescriptions.Nodejs:
## Node.js

My main server runtime. I've built everything from simple automation scripts to high-traffic APIs processing thousands of requests per second.

### Typical stack
- **Frameworks**: Express, Fastify, Hono (Edge-compatible).
- **Streaming**: Node.js Streams for file and large data processing.
- **Workers**: `worker_threads` for CPU-intensive tasks without blocking the event loop.
- **Monitoring**: integration with OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing.

### Best practices
I design my services with structured error handling, logging with `pino`, and input validation at each layer.
skillDescriptions.Go:
## Go

Language I've explored for high-performance microservices where Node.js wasn't sufficient. I fell in love with its simplicity and goroutines.

### What I've built
- Image processing microservice with parallel concurrency via goroutines.
- Internal CLI tools for deployment automation.
- REST APIs with `net/http` + `chi` router.

### Learning in progress
I continue to deepen my understanding of Go concurrency patterns (channels, select, context cancellation) and the native testing ecosystem.
skillDescriptions.GraphQL:
## GraphQL

I've worked with GraphQL both on the server and client side, in projects where query flexibility was a requirement.

### Server experience
- Schemas with resolvers in Node.js using Apollo Server and graphql-yoga.
- **DataLoader** to efficiently solve the N+1 problem.
- Authentication with custom directives (`@auth`, `@hasRole`).

### Client experience
- Apollo Client with normalized cache and optimistic updates.
- Code generation with `graphql-codegen` for automatic TypeScript types.

### When I choose it
GraphQL shines when multiple clients (web, mobile) need different data from the same backend.
skillDescriptions.RESTAPIs:
## REST APIs

REST API design is something I pay special attention to: making them intuitive, predictable, and well-documented.

### Principles I follow
- **Well-named resources** and HTTP verbs used correctly.
- **API versioning** (`/v1/`, `/v2/`) to avoid breaking existing clients.
- **Structured errors**: I always return a body with `code`, `message` and optionally `details`.
- **Pagination**: cursor-based for large lists, page-based for dashboards.

### Documentation
I use OpenAPI/Swagger to document API contracts, with automatic request validation via Zod.
skillDescriptions.tRPC:
## tRPC

One of my favorite technologies in recent years. It eliminates friction between frontend and backend with real end-to-end type-safety.

### How I use it
- **Monorepos** with Next.js: the tRPC router lives in the App Router with Route Handlers.
- **Middleware** for authentication and context injection (session, database).
- **Subscriptions** with SSE for real-time feeds.
- Input validation with Zod in each procedure.

### Why I recommend it
With tRPC, a signature change in the backend produces a TypeScript error in the frontend instantly. No more broken contracts at runtime.
skillDescriptions.EdgeFunctions:
## Edge Functions

Distributed compute that runs close to the user. I use it to reduce latency in features that don't need to access a central database.

### Use cases I've implemented
- **Authentication middleware** on Vercel Edge: JWT verification without cold start.
- **A/B testing**: variant redirection without the user seeing a flash.
- **Geo-routing**: serving different content based on user region.
- **Lightweight rate limiting** with counters in Upstash Redis.

### Limitations to keep in mind
The Edge Runtime has a subset of Node.js APIs. Not everything that works in Node.js works on Edge.
skillDescriptions.PostgreSQL:
## PostgreSQL

My reference relational database. I choose Postgres almost always for its reliability, powerful query planner, and extensions.

### What I handle with ease
- **Schema design**: normalization, relationships, constraints, and strategic indexes.
- **Advanced queries**: CTEs, window functions, JSON aggregation, full-text search.
- **Migrations**: management with Prisma Migrate or Flyway in legacy projects.
- **Connection pooling** with PgBouncer or Neon's built-in pooler.

### Favorite extensions
`pgvector` for semantic search, `PostGIS` for geospatial data, `pg_cron` for scheduled tasks.
skillDescriptions.Redis:
## Redis

I use it as a cache layer and message broker in architectures where latency matters.

### Applied use cases
- **API response cache**: reducing database load with dynamic TTL.
- **Session store**: storing user sessions with automatic expiration.
- **Rate limiting**: counters per IP/user with `INCR` + `EXPIRE`.
- **Job queues**: with BullMQ to process background tasks (emails, webhooks).

### Services used
Upstash Redis (serverless), Redis Cloud and local Redis via Docker in development.
skillDescriptions.Prisma:
## Prisma

ORM that has transformed how I work with databases. The combination of declarative schema + automatically generated types is unbeatable.

### Workflow
1. I define the schema in `schema.prisma` with models and relationships.
2. `prisma migrate dev` generates and applies the SQL migration.
3. The generated client has 100% correct types, no need to write them manually.

### Advanced features
- **Interactive transactions** with `prisma.$transaction`.
- **Prisma middleware** for logging, soft-deletes and auditing.
- **Raw queries** with `$queryRawUnsafe` when the query planner needs a hint.
- Integration with Zod via `zod-prisma-types` for automatic validation.
skillDescriptions.Docker:
## Docker

Indispensable tool for having reproducible development environments and packaging applications consistently.

### Daily use
- **docker-compose** to spin up local stacks: Postgres, Redis, custom services.
- **Multi-stage builds** for small and secure production images.
- **.dockerignore** and optimized layers for fast CI builds.

### In production
I've deployed containers on ECS (Fargate), Railway and Fly.io. The consistency between environments that Docker offers is its greatest value.
skillDescriptions.AWS:
## AWS

I've worked with the most common AWS services in medium-scale projects, without being a dedicated cloud architect.

### Services I've used
- **S3**: asset storage, user uploads and backups.
- **CloudFront**: CDN in front of S3 and custom origins.
- **ECS / Fargate**: container deployment without managing servers.
- **SES**: sending transactional emails at scale.
- **Lambda**: serverless functions for webhooks and async processing.

### Tools
AWS CDK for infrastructure as code, and AWS Console for monitoring and troubleshooting.
skillDescriptions.Vercel:
## Vercel

My preferred deployment platform for Next.js projects. The integration is so fluid that deployment almost feels invisible.

### What I leverage
- **Preview Deployments**: each PR has its own environment. Stakeholders can review before merging.
- **Edge Network**: assets and Edge Functions in over 100 points of presence.
- **Analytics and Speed Insights**: real metrics of Core Web Vitals.
- **Cron Jobs**: scheduled tasks without needing a dedicated server.

### Advanced configuration
I handle `vercel.json` for rewrites, custom cache headers and per-region function configuration.
skillDescriptions.Git:
## Git

Beyond `commit`, `push` and `pull`. Git is a communication and collaboration tool when used well.

### Practices I apply
- **Conventional Commits**: structured messages that enable automatic changelogs.
- **Feature branches** with small, focused PRs that are easy to review.
- **Interactive rebase**: clean and linear history before merging.
- **Git hooks** with Husky: automatic lint and tests on pre-commit and pre-push.

### Workflows
I've worked with GitHub Flow (continuous deployments) and variants of Gitflow (versioned releases) depending on project context.
skillDescriptions.CICD:
## CI/CD

Continuous integration and deployment pipelines that ensure code reaching production always passes necessary checks.

### What I configure in my pipelines
- **Lint + type check** on each PR to block code with errors.
- **Test suite** (unit + integration) with coverage report.
- **Build + deploy** automatic to staging on each merge to `main`.
- **Automatic release** to production with manual or automatic approval.

### Platforms
Primarily **GitHub Actions**, I've also used GitLab CI and CircleCI. I know security best practices: secrets in vault, minimum permissions on tokens.
skillDescriptions.Vitest:
## Vitest

My testing framework for modern projects with Vite/Next.js. Extremely fast thanks to HMR and native ESM compatibility.

### How I structure tests
- **Unit tests**: pure functions, hooks and utilities with high coverage.
- **Component tests**: with `@testing-library/react` to validate UI behavior.
- **Mocking**: `vi.mock` to isolate external dependencies (APIs, system modules).

### Testing philosophy
I don't blindly pursue 100% coverage. I focus on testing observable behavior, not internal implementation.
skillDescriptions.Playwright:
## Playwright

End-to-end testing framework I use to validate critical user flows before each release.

### Tests I implement with Playwright
- **Authentication flows**: signup, login, password recovery.
- **Critical business flows**: checkout, resource creation, data export.
- **Cross-browser**: Chrome, Firefox and WebKit in the same test suite.

### CI integration
Playwright tests run in GitHub Actions in parallel, with screenshot and video artifacts when they fail to facilitate debugging.
skillDescriptions.DesignSystems:
## Design Systems

I've built and maintained design systems from scratch, as well as integrated existing systems (shadcn/ui, Radix, Material) in real projects.

### What it means to me
- **Design tokens**: colors, typography, spacing and radii as CSS variables or Tailwind config.
- **Polymorphic components**: `Button`, `Input`, `Dialog` that adapt to any context.
- **Documentation**: stories in Storybook + MDX so designers and devs speak the same language.
- **Versioning**: publishing internal packages with semantic versioning.

### Real value
A good design system multiplies team speed and guarantees visual consistency without extra effort.
skillDescriptions.Observability:
## Observability

The difference between knowing something is broken when a user calls, and knowing it before it affects anyone.

### The three pillars
- **Logs**: structured JSON logging with `pino`, centralized in Datadog or Loki.
- **Metrics**: API latency, error rate and saturation. Dashboards in Grafana.
- **Traces**: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry to understand flow between services.

### Alerts
I configure alerts with sensible thresholds (not too noisy, not too quiet) for the service's most critical SLOs.

fleet-control.description: An internal platform I conceived, developed, and deployed for ETI to inspect Docker infrastructure, generate reports, and manage maintenance. It integrates Portainer, Nextcloud, scheduled cleanup, and updates with simulation, approvals, and recovery. I also built the CI/CD with GitLab, Nexus, and Docker Swarm, and continue to support it on the company servers.
highlights: Identified an internal need and owned the full lifecycle: product definition, architecture, full-stack development, data modeling, CI/CD, deployment, and ongoing support.
Integrated Portainer for environment and container inventories with URL-based filters, and Excel exports archived to Nextcloud through WebDAV.
Implemented cleanup policies per environment with retention, manual confirmation, daily scheduling, and persistent execution results and reclaimed-space history.
Coordinated concurrent tasks and recovered interrupted execution records using transactions, unique constraints, atomic claiming, and renewable execution leases.
Built Docker application updates with simulation, major-version approval, backups, health checks, and rollback mechanisms.
Prepared delivery through GitLab CI/CD, Nexus, and Docker Swarm: multi-stage images, migrations before deployment, service verification, and manual recovery tools.
Deployed the solution to production on ETI servers and continue to maintain and support it after delivery.
fleet-control.technicalNotes:
## Context, Ownership, and Responsibility

I created **Fleet Control from scratch at ETI, starting development in 2026**, to address a company need: inspecting Docker infrastructure, preparing reports, and organizing maintenance through an internal tool. Portainer already provided access to the environments; my proposal added workflows tailored to internal operations.

I owned the concept, module and workflow definition, architecture, frontend, backend, data model, and integrations. I also prepared CI/CD, deployed the application on the company servers, and took responsibility for ongoing support. The solution is **deployed and operational**, with maintenance under my responsibility.

## Inventory and Operational Documentation

The application queries Portainer environments and their containers. It presents environment status, type, groups, tags, and connection information, along with container images, ports, and creation dates. Search, filters, sorting, and pagination narrow each query; URL-based filters preserve context and let another authorized user open the same view. The interface handles loading, empty results, and integration errors.

Inventories can be exported to **server-generated Excel** with the generation date and applied filters. Exports use the filtered dataset, up to 10,000 records, rather than only the visible page. In addition to delivering the file to the browser, the system attempts to archive it in **Nextcloud through WebDAV**, creating directories as needed.

An archival failure is logged and can still allow the download to complete. The response waits for the attempt, so a slow Nextcloud instance can add latency. Cleanup reports use a separate mechanism: they are reconstructed from persisted data and downloaded as text, without being archived to Nextcloud.

## Cleanup Policies, History, and Recovery

Docker Cleanup supports a daily time, **1–365 days of retention**, and resource selection per environment. Cleanup is limited to stopped containers, unused images, and build cache, with the corresponding retention filters; volumes and networks are excluded. Manual runs require a written confirmation specific to the selected environment.

Each task retains a policy snapshot, its manual or scheduled origin, the requesting user when applicable, and results by resource. History shows states, deletions, reclaimed space, and errors, and offers a report reconstructed from PostgreSQL.

I separated **persistent task reservation from execution**: an action records pending work, responds, and schedules processing through Next.js after(). The executor claims it with an atomic transition from PENDING to RUNNING; the interface refreshes history while work remains active. Results survive even if another phase fails.

An external scheduler calls the protected cleanup endpoint, intended every minute. The server reserves due policies and returns **202 Accepted**. Scheduling uses **America/New_York**, with deterministic handling of nonexistent or repeated local times around daylight-saving transitions. Environment/local-date constraints prevent duplicate daily occurrences, while another constraint prevents two active cleanups for the same environment.

Serializable transactions and renewable leases coordinate concurrency. A running task renews a 20-minute lease before its phases. If the process is interrupted and the lease expires, reconciliation retains confirmed results and identifies uncertain phases. **Destructive requests with ambiguous outcomes are not automatically retried**: losing a response does not establish that Docker never executed the operation.

## Controlled Application Updates

Docker Updates includes initial configurations for **GitLab CE, Portainer CE, and Sonatype Nexus 3**, and supports configuring other compatible applications. It identifies the running version through Compose or Swarm, queries Docker Hub or Registry API v2-compatible registries, and selects versions using configurable rules, excluding references such as latest and prereleases recognized by its filters.

- Minor and patch updates can run manually or automatically.
- A major-version jump creates an approval request; approval rechecks that the starting version still matches the reviewed one.
- Simulation records the comparison and intended decision without updating services or creating backups.
- Automatic execution is enabled per application and is off by default.

Before making changes, the executor acquires a lock in the backup directory and copies configured paths and the Compose file. GitLab also has support for its native backup tool. The executor pins the version in Compose, updates the service, and waits for a successful health response when a URL is configured. For Portainer, it coordinates Server and Agent.

On failure, it attempts to restore backed-up data, the previous image, and configuration. History distinguishes completed updates, simulations, pending approvals, **ROLLED_BACK**, and **CRITICAL** when recovery also fails. Rollback effectiveness depends on each application, backup consistency, paths, and permissions; it does not guarantee restoration.

A scheduler service without Docker socket access calls the endpoint with a dedicated secret. It only considers enabled applications and records at most one scheduled run per application and UTC date. Notifications can use a Slack webhook or the Telegram API.

## Architecture, Integrations, and Persistence

I designed a **modular monolith with Next.js, React, and TypeScript**, organized by feature. Server Components participate in initial reads; client components handle forms and interaction. Server Actions and HTTP endpoints delegate logic to module services.

For inventory and cleanup, the backend acts as a **BFF**: Portainer credentials remain on the server and the browser receives normalized contracts. Zod schemas and mappers handle optional fields, nulls, and external response variations. Updates use a different integration path: Docker CLI with access to the socket and mounted configuration and backup paths.

~~~text
Internal users → React / Next.js → Access controls and module services
  → Portainer client → Environments and Docker Engines
  → ExcelJS → Download + WebDAV archival attempt in Nextcloud
  → Updates → Registry + Docker CLI / Compose / Swarm
  → PostgreSQL / Prisma → Sessions, policies, runs, and approvals

Schedulers → Endpoints with dedicated secrets → Maintenance
GitLab CI/CD → Nexus Registry → Migrations → Docker Swarm
~~~

Portainer is the inventory source. **PostgreSQL and Prisma** retain users, accounts, sessions, policies, runs, results, configured applications, and approvals. The database also coordinates cleanup reservations through constraints and transactions.

Better Auth manages persisted sessions. Public signup is disabled and accounts are created through internal administration. The model distinguishes **viewer** and **admin**, with administrative navigation and inventory/report access for both roles. User management includes checks to preserve at least one active administrator and prevent administrators from deleting their own account or changing their own access.

### Technologies and Responsibilities

| Area | Technologies and purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Application | Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript: routes, rendering, and full-stack logic. |
| Interface | Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Radix UI, Lucide, and TanStack Table: forms, tables, and navigation. |
| Contracts and languages | React Hook Form, Zod, next-intl: validation, normalization, and an ES/EN internationalization foundation. |
| Identity and data | Better Auth, PostgreSQL, Prisma 7: sessions, relational modeling, migrations, and history. |
| Integrations | Portainer REST API, Docker Engine API, ExcelJS, Nextcloud/WebDAV: inventory, cleanup, and reports. |
| Automation | Node.js, Docker CLI, Compose, Swarm, tar, Registry API v2: versions, updates, and backups. |
| Transport | Fetch and Undici: integrations, timeouts, and proxy support. |
| Delivery and quality | GitLab CI/CD, Nexus, multi-stage Dockerfile, Vitest, ESLint, and TypeScript. |

## CI/CD, Deployment, and Ongoing Support

I prepared a pipeline with five stages: **build, push, update, verify, and notify**. It builds an image with a tag identifying the build, publishes it to Nexus, and generates runtime configuration from CI/CD variables.

Before updating the Docker Swarm stack, a dedicated container applies Prisma migrations and can initialize the first administrator when configured. The multi-stage image separates dependencies, build, migration, and runtime; the application uses Next.js standalone output. Separating migrations from service startup allows them to run once per deployment.

Checks inspect the service, replicas, deployed image, HTTP connectivity, and recent logs. Notifications use a server script when available. Manual jobs inspect status and request rollback of Fleet Control itself; this deployment mechanism is separate from Docker Updates' application recovery.

My responsibility continues after releasing a version: I maintain the solution and provide support on the servers where I deployed it.

## Engineering Challenges, Quality, and Scope

Challenges included normalizing variable Docker and Portainer responses, preserving partial results, coordinating manual and scheduled requests, and adapting service discovery to Compose and Swarm. Long-running operations also required adjusting Undici transport limits: extending AbortController alone does not prevent another timeout from closing the connection.

The supplied project material describes specifications, business rules, edge cases, and traceability, plus unit tests for access, normalization, retention, absence of destructive retries, reports, daylight-saving transitions, and version policies. Test, lint, and type-check commands exist; **they are not yet mandatory pipeline stages**, and deployment checks do not constitute exhaustive validation. Adding this portfolio case is not a new execution of those tests or a production audit.

The solution delivers searchable inventory, reusable documentation, and maintenance procedures with history. The ES/EN foundation and access controls still need consistent coverage across modules; recovery requires validation per application. I do not claim savings percentages, guaranteed availability, or incident reductions without measurements.

My contribution combines **autonomy to conceive the product, ability to build it, and responsibility for its operation**. History and the pipeline provide a basis for later measuring reclaimed space, maintenance outcomes, report preparation time, and release delivery time.

gestionvc.description: I conceived and built a platform from scratch for ETI that turns TrueConf records into usage and charges per company. I developed the Next.js frontend and NestJS API, integrated PostgreSQL and Redis, and implemented access controls and Excel reports. I also prepared CI/CD with GitLab, Nexus, and Docker Swarm, deployed the solution, and continue providing support on the company's servers.
highlights: Identified ETI's need and conceived the solution from scratch, taking responsibility for product definition, architecture, data modeling, and full-stack development.
Built two independent services with Next.js and NestJS to centralize companies, rates, users, usage, and information supporting billing.
Integrated TrueConf through its REST API and OAuth 2.0 and implemented accumulated usage and per-company charge calculations for usage-based and flat-rate plans.
Optimized queries through monthly preloading in Redis, in-memory data reuse, and concurrency limits to moderate the load on TrueConf.
Implemented role-based access, web sessions, password recovery, user and group administration, a dashboard, and Excel exports.
Prepared Docker images and separate pipelines for both services with GitLab CI/CD, Nexus Registry, Docker Swarm deployment, verification, and manual rollback.
Started development in September 2025, deployed the solution to production, and continue maintaining its operation and providing support on ETI's servers.
gestionvc.technicalNotes:
## Need, Authorship, and Responsibility

I started **GestionVC in September 2025** to address a need at ETI: connect usage of its TrueConf videoconferencing service with the companies using it, their rate plans, and the charges for each period. I turned that need into a dedicated platform for usage management and billing support.

I conceived the product and took responsibility for its technical design, data model, frontend, backend, and integrations. I also prepared CI/CD, deployed it on the company's servers, and continue providing support. The project runs from **September 2025–present**, with the solution in production and ongoing support under my responsibility.

TrueConf provides the communication infrastructure and records. My work was to incorporate ETI's rules: billable companies, rate plans, usage attribution, permissions, and reports for the people managing the service.

## Architecture and Data Responsibilities

I organized the solution into **two deployable services, each with its own repository, image, and pipeline**. The Next.js application communicates with the NestJS API over HTTP REST using the session JWT; the backend owns the business rules and integrations.

| System | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Next.js 16 and React 19 | Interface, navigation, web session, server components and functions; authorized intermediary for report downloads. |
| NestJS 11 and TypeORM 0.3 | Modular REST API, data access, usage and charge calculations, TrueConf integration, and scheduled tasks. |
| PostgreSQL 17 | Companies, rates, GestionVC accounts, and the integration token with its expiration information. |
| TrueConf Server | Service users and groups, communications, and participation records. |
| Redis 7 and ioredis 5 | Precalculated usage, recovery tokens, and password-change timestamps. |
| SMTP and Nodemailer | Delivery of password recovery instructions. |

I separated the backend into modules for authentication, companies, rates, management accounts, TrueConf users, groups, calls, participants, billing, general information, and reports. This lets lists, indicators, and exports reuse the same calculations. During processing, I also reuse the token and user and company lookups through in-memory maps.

## Companies, Rates, and Usage Calculations

Administrators can register companies, mark them as billable, assign a rate, and configure a user limit to monitor service usage. The model associates one rate with several companies and each company with its GestionVC accounts. I prevented deletion of assigned rates and added interface validation requiring a rate when a company is marked as billable.

I implemented two options: **usage-based rates**, with price and time-unit plans for video calls and symmetric or asymmetric conferences, and **flat rates**, with a fixed monthly price.

For each period, I retrieve communication records, resolve the owner and their company in TrueConf, fetch participants, and add their durations. I then classify the communication, apply the appropriate plan, and aggregate the results by company. The general query combines information for billable companies.

**Usage means accumulated participation time.** Three participants connected for ten minutes produce thirty minutes of usage even though the meeting lasts ten minutes. The communication is attributed to its owner's company.

```text
usage = sum of participation durations
charge = round to 2 decimal places(
  usage in seconds × plan price / plan base seconds
)
```

For flat rates, the charge per call is zero and the summary includes the company's fixed fee once. Queries show usage, charges, video call and conference counts, and an average based on accumulated usage and counted communications.

The module supports billing information; its scope does not include fiscal invoice issuance, payment collection, or accounting reconciliation. The fixed fee is not automatically prorated when querying a period other than a month.

## TrueConf Integration and Optimization

I implemented OAuth 2.0 with `client_credentials`, token persistence in PostgreSQL, expiration checks, and in-memory reuse. Token retrieval runs at application startup and through a scheduled task.

For queries using the request helper, I added timeouts and retries with exponential backoff for network errors or aborts. I also adapted identifiers, parameters, responses, and provider errors to present useful messages, including existing-name conflicts. Date handling includes conversions between UTC and **America/Havana**, which matter when defining usage periods.

Enriching a call can require several external requests. To avoid repeating that work for common monthly queries, I implemented preloading for the current and previous months: it is attempted at startup and refreshed **every ten minutes**. Results are stored in Redis with a configurable lifetime of **fifteen minutes by default**.

Compatible queries reuse the result and apply filters and limits locally. When data is missing or the requested period needs a different path, the application queries the source directly. The refresh interval balances data freshness and the load on TrueConf.

I limited call-processing concurrency to **three tasks** and certain group membership operations to **five**. I also developed reusable Redis utilities for querying and storing results, pattern-based invalidation with `SCAN`, interceptors, and decorators; monthly preloading uses the Redis service directly.

## Administration, Access, and User Experience

The platform distinguishes GestionVC accounts from TrueConf service accounts. GestionVC users belong to a company and have an operator, administrator, or superadministrator role. Through the provider API, I implemented creation, editing, deletion, avatars, and group membership for TrueConf users.

The per-company user count traverses the API's pages and supports comparison with the configured limit. The panel brings technical administration and its business context together.

The backend validates credentials and issues a JWT. The frontend maintains the session through **iron-session** and a sealed cookie with `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, and `Secure` in production. The API requires authentication by default through a global guard, explicitly declares public endpoints, and applies role controls and company filters to the corresponding queries.

The JWT strategy checks that the user exists and retrieves their role and company from the database. Recovery uses a temporary token in Redis, SMTP email, and deletion of the used token. Password-change timestamps allow older JWTs to be rejected. I complemented these mechanisms with bcrypt, Helmet, request limits, and centralized exception handling.

For the interface, I used **Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, and Radix UI**, forms with React Hook Form and Zod, and reusable tables with TanStack Table. Filters and pagination are represented in the URL, alongside column preferences, loading states, confirmations, and notifications. Parallel and intercepted routes display selected forms and details in modals while preserving list context.

## Dashboard and Reports

The dashboard combines company, user, usage, and charge indicators. Recharts visualizations show video calls and conferences, users by role, plans in use, and companies approaching their account limit. I separated general information and billing blocks through **Suspense** so they can load and display results independently.

I integrated **Excel export with ExcelJS**. A Next.js Route Handler acts as an intermediary, adds authorization, and preserves file headers; a shared hook coordinates downloads and notifications.

The backend also includes templates and endpoints for **PDF generation with Puppeteer**. This capability is distinct from the Excel export flow connected to the interface.

## CI/CD, Deployment, and Operations

I prepared a GitLab pipeline for each service with the flow **Build → Push → Update → Verify → Notify**. It builds the application and Docker image, generates a temporary tag, publishes to Nexus Registry, prepares configuration, and deploys or updates the service in Docker Swarm.

Verification inspects status, replicas, deployed image, connectivity, and recent logs. Notification invokes the server's mechanism when available. I included manual actions to inspect status and request service rollback. These checks provide operational visibility; their scope differs from a functional test suite.

The images use multi-stage builds. The frontend uses `standalone` output and runs as a non-root user. Services share a Swarm network, while PostgreSQL and Redis have persistent volumes, health checks, and, for Redis, AOF persistence.

Infrastructure includes memory limits and reservations, restart and update policies, and scripts that wait for PostgreSQL and Redis before starting the API. I also adapted environment configuration and certificates to ETI's infrastructure. I personally deployed the solution to production and maintain support for the running system.

## Value for ETI and Continuity

GestionVC centralizes companies, rates, users, and usage; applies shared calculation rules; and lets staff review the communications behind aggregated charges. Excel exports make this information available by company and period, while preloading reuses completed processing.

The main challenges were translating technical records into economic rules, controlling the cost of an integration requiring multiple queries, and maintaining a consistent interface across modules. The project demonstrates my ability to **conceive a solution, build it, and take responsibility for its operation**.

These benefits describe implemented capabilities. Measuring administrative time saved, latency reductions, or handled volume requires operational data; I do not claim percentages or impact figures without those measurements.

sicom.tagline: Commercial analytics and operations platform for ETI
sicom.description: In response to a need communicated to me by ETI’s Commercial department, I conceived and started a platform from scratch, bringing together billing, commercial management and accounting information from three enterprise systems. When another developer joined to focus primarily on the API, I took responsibility for the web client and its integration, shared business logic decisions and implemented authentication and email delivery. I prepared CI/CD, deployed SICOM on ETI’s servers and continue to provide support.
sicom.teamSize: Solution conception and two-person development team
highlights: ETI’s Commercial department contacted me and communicated its need; I conceived SICOM and began development from scratch in October 2025.
After the initial versions, continued building the product with another developer: he focused primarily on the API and I on the web client, with shared business logic decisions.
Developed and integrated screens, filters, forms, indicators, lists, consolidated entity views and exports against the API contracts.
Implemented authentication, sessions, token renewal, password changes, account recovery and email delivery.
Integrated the web experience for querying MISTRAL, RECOM and SISCONT information and reviewing pending relationships between entities.
The product also incorporates delivery points, dispatchers, orders, documents and commission charges as an evolving extension.
Prepared CI/CD with GitLab, Nexus and Docker Swarm and deployed the Web and API services on ETI’s servers.
From October 2025 to the present, I have accompanied SICOM’s evolution and continue to support the deployed solution.
sicom.technicalNotes:
## The need, the initiative and the team’s evolution

I started **SICOM in October 2025** after the Commercial department of **Empresa de Tecnología de la Información (ETI)** contacted me and communicated its need to query and connect information spread across billing, commercial management and accounting tools. The project runs from **October 2025–present**; it is deployed on ETI’s servers and I continue to provide support.

Everyday questions—how much has been billed, which service requests remain open, which contracts are approaching expiry and which balances remain outstanding—required visiting different sources and comparing results. The same entity could appear under different names or codes, adding manual work to the analysis.

I conceived the solution and developed its first versions. Another developer then joined, and we divided the main responsibilities: **he took ownership primarily of the API service and I of the web client**. We shared business logic decisions and coordinated integration. I implemented authentication and email delivery, prepared CI/CD and performed the deployment.

The capabilities and architecture described here belong to the collaboratively built product. Data integration modules and API business logic form part of that joint work; my responsibility combines solution conception, web development and integration, security, delivery and support.

## A common entry point for commercial information

SICOM brings together three systems with different responsibilities and provides views for exploring their data from a common perspective.

| Source | Information provided | Database |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **MISTRAL** | Billing, sales, customers, services, service lines and warehouses. | SQL Server |
| **RECOM** | Customers, service requests and contracts. | PostgreSQL |
| **SISCONT** | Income, accounts receivable and payable, and advance payments. | SQL Server |

The dashboard presents billing indicators, open requests, contracts approaching expiry, income and consolidated entities. It also reflects source availability and lets users continue their analysis in the detail modules.

| Area | Product capabilities | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing | Indicators, filters, sorting, pagination and Excel export. | Find the records behind a result by period, customer, warehouse, service line, service, customer type or contract. |
| Commercial management | Requests and contracts, summaries and expiry windows of 30, 60 and 90 days. | Follow up on requests and identify contracts requiring attention. |
| Finance | Income, accounts receivable and payable, advance payments and balance ageing. | Bring the accounting perspective into commercial analysis. |
| Consolidated information | Customer, service line and warehouse catalogues and detail views. | Examine an entity across multiple sources. |
| Administration | Users, roles, account status, profiles and account recovery. | Organise access to the system’s capabilities. |

## Consolidation and data quality

Bringing information together requires determining which records represent the same entity. SICOM stores **mappings between source identifiers** and uses code, document and name matching strategies adapted to each domain.

Ambiguous cases become pending relationships. An administrator can review source information and suggestions, complete a mapping, dismiss a pending case or associate certain codes as variants of an already linked customer. These relationships are stored in SICOM’s own database and guide subsequent queries.

A consolidated customer view allows navigation between billing, requests, contracts, accounts receivable and advance payments according to the recorded mappings. My web integration work included representing both available relationships and states requiring review.

Human review is part of the workflow: the quality of a mapping determines how much a user can trust a consolidated query.

## The web experience and analysis workflows

I organised and integrated screens with filters, forms, lists, summaries and actions connected to the API. The frontend combines **Server Components for initial views** with Client Components for filters, selection, dialogs and forms. Each functional module brings together components, hooks, actions, services and types.

For billing analysis, the user selects a period and relevant criteria; **filters are represented in the URL**, preserving the query across reloads and allowing it to be shared with another authorised user. Users can then sort, paginate and generate an Excel file with the active filters, retrieving the pages required for the report.

Remote catalogues support search, pagination and incremental loading. The client prevents earlier responses from overwriting newer results and presents loading, empty and error states. Growing catalogues can therefore be used without downloading every option at once.

Integration also requires distinguishing consolidated identifiers from source codes and explicitly adapting filters and list, summary and export contracts. I coordinated these decisions with the API developer to keep screen behaviour consistent with the meaning of the data.

## Architecture and separation of responsibilities

The product uses a **pnpm monorepo with two deployable applications**: a Next.js Web application and a modular NestJS API.

~~~text
User
   |
   v
Next.js Web
   |-- Screens, filters, forms and navigation
   |-- Server and interactive components
   |-- BFF: session and authenticated API access
   |
   v
NestJS API
   |-- Authentication, permissions and auditing
   |-- Information queries and consolidation
   |-- Delivery points, orders and charges
   |
   |-- MISTRAL / SQL Server ........ read access
   |-- RECOM / PostgreSQL .......... read access
   |-- SISCONT / SQL Server ........ read access
   |
   +-- SICOM / PostgreSQL .......... own persistence

Supporting services: SMTP and file storage.
Deployment: Web and API images on Docker Swarm.
~~~

MISTRAL, RECOM and SISCONT connections are used for queries, with automatic schema synchronisation disabled. SICOM’s own database stores users, sessions, audit records, mappings, pending relationships and its operational data, and evolves through migrations.

Next.js also acts as a **Backend for Frontend (BFF)**. Server-only services concentrate communication with the API, while Server Actions receive operations initiated from the interface. REST contracts are documented through Swagger/OpenAPI in development; the client adapts them through explicit services and types.

This separation supports new capabilities while maintaining a clear boundary with the systems already supporting ETI’s operations.

## Authentication, authorisation and email

I implemented the access lifecycle as a responsibility spanning the interface, server and persistence. The Web application stores its session in an **HttpOnly cookie encrypted with JWE**: its server obtains the tokens needed to call the API, while interface JavaScript cannot read the cookie’s contents. Configuration covers SameSite and Secure according to the environment.

The mechanisms include **Argon2id** passwords, mandatory initial password changes, JWT access tokens, rotating refresh tokens, revocation based on account status and authorisation version, persistent request limits and audit events with correlation identifiers. Refresh token reuse handling includes bounded idempotent recovery for certain retries.

Authorisation distinguishes **ADMINISTRADOR, COMERCIAL and DESPACHADOR** roles. Navigation adapts to the role and the API validates permissions; order operations also check the dispatcher’s assignment to the delivery point.

Account recovery connects security and email:

1. The request returns a generic response and, when it corresponds to an active account, sends a link over SMTP using Nodemailer.
2. The link contains an expiring random token; the database stores its hash.
3. The user sets a new password with a single-use token.
4. The operation invalidates recovery links and existing sessions.
5. The user signs in again with the new credentials.

The workflow handles repeated requests, expired links and email transport failures. It includes localised templates and messages that avoid revealing whether an account exists.

## Extending into deliveries, orders and charges

SICOM incorporates an operational area for the delivery service ETI provides to e-commerce stores. This data belongs to its own database. The extension is implemented in the project and **continues to evolve**; tracking documentation still lists the order requirement as in progress.

It includes delivery points, dispatcher assignments, originating stores, manual order entry and PDF imports with format-specific parsers. The dispatcher enters an assigned point, selects the store, records or imports an order, then reviews and corrects the data before confirming it.

Orders support downloading the original PDF and generating warranty documents in Excel. For external providers, the system groups orders from the same store and currency to calculate ETI’s commission charge, records the percentage and amount per order and checks whether orders are already associated with a charge. The resulting invoice can be downloaded as a PDF.

This commission workflow has a specific purpose within delivery management.

## CI/CD, deployment and ongoing support

I prepared automated delivery and brought the platform into operation on ETI’s servers. **GitLab CI/CD builds and publishes the Web and API images to Nexus and updates the Docker Swarm stack**.

The pipeline uses commit-associated image tags, prepares configuration, runs migrations and entity reconciliation from that version’s code and checks services, replicas, running images and HTTP responses. Migration tasks are serialised through a resource group.

The Dockerfiles use multiple stages, pinned Node.js and pnpm versions and lockfile-based dependency installation. The Web application uses Next.js standalone output, and both images run the application as the node user.

The stack configures healthchecks, memory limits, restart policies and updates with rollback on failure. Checks and recorded deployment results provide information for diagnosing operational issues. My responsibility continues through maintenance and support of the deployed solution.

## Engineering challenges, technologies and quality

One challenge was preserving the meaning of data from its source to the screen: resolving differing identities, representing ambiguity and coordinating contract changes with the API. Another was completing the session lifecycle, including expiry, renewal, concurrent requests, password changes and revocation.

Amounts require precision and correct interpretation. The product uses **decimal strings**, decimal.js in the API and commission calculations in cents with **BigInt**; the client also provides utilities for summing and formatting decimal strings. An invoice lacking a matching accounting record does not, by itself, establish that it has been paid.

| Area | Technologies and application |
| --- | --- |
| Language and organisation | TypeScript, Node.js and pnpm workspaces. |
| Web and BFF | Next.js 16, React 19, App Router, server rendering and Server Actions. |
| Interface and languages | Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Radix UI, Lucide and next-intl for Spanish and English. |
| Forms | React Hook Form and Zod for form state and validation. |
| API and data | NestJS 11, TypeORM, class-validator, Swagger/OpenAPI, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and parameterised SQL. |
| Security and email | JWT, JOSE/JWE, Argon2id, Node.js cryptographic primitives, Nodemailer and SMTP. |
| Documents and calculations | ExcelJS, pdf-parse, PDFKit, decimal.js, BigInt and decimal string utilities. |
| Quality | Vitest, Testing Library, Jest, Supertest, ESLint and TypeScript. |
| Delivery | Docker, Docker Swarm, GitLab CI/CD and Nexus. |

The SICOM repository includes tests covering authorisation, session encryption, password changes and recovery, filter normalisation, entity matching, PDF parsing and monetary calculations. Each application combines tests, type checks, lint and compilation; the root pnpm verify command detects affected workspaces. API integration and end-to-end tests have separate commands because they require external services.

## Value for ETI and continued development

SICOM provides a common entry point for information that previously required visiting several tools. It supports analysis by source and entity, examination of contracts and balances requiring follow-up, report generation and progressive review of relationships between systems. The delivery extension adds operational workflows and documents to that foundation.

The result is a platform integrating **three source systems**, organising access through **three roles** and bringing together queries, analysis, exports and operations. Time savings and error reductions require usage measurements; I describe delivered capabilities without assigning improvement percentages.

My contribution demonstrates the ability to **understand a business need, turn it into a product, build collaboratively and take responsibility for delivery and support**. SICOM continues to evolve with my participation and ongoing support.

vercel-ai-sdk.tagline: Streaming and provider integrations for edge-ready AI applications
vercel-ai-sdk.description: Contributed streaming improvements and new provider adapters to the official Vercel AI SDK, improving edge-runtime compatibility.
vercel-ai-sdk.impact: Reduced streaming latency by ~30% on edge runtimes across all provider adapters.
vercel-ai-sdk.technicalNotes:
## What I contributed

The Vercel AI SDK's streaming layer used Node.js `Readable` streams internally, which aren't available on edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge). I refactored the core streaming abstraction to use the **Web Streams API** (`ReadableStream`) as the primary interface, with a Node.js compatibility shim.

## Provider adapter

Added a new adapter for **Anthropic's Messages API**, including support for tool-use streaming and prompt caching headers.

radix-ui-primitives.tagline: Accessibility fixes for keyboard and screen reader users
radix-ui-primitives.description: Fixed accessibility regressions in Dialog and Tooltip components, added keyboard-navigation spec tests, and improved WAI-ARIA compliance.
radix-ui-primitives.impact: Resolved 3 long-standing WCAG violations affecting screen reader users across all Radix consumers.
radix-ui-primitives.technicalNotes:
## Focus management bug

On iOS Safari, `Dialog` was not restoring focus to the trigger after close because the browser's focus behavior differs from the spec. Fixed by explicitly storing the trigger ref and calling `.focus()` in a `requestAnimationFrame` callback after the close animation completes.

## ARIA cleanup

`Tooltip` was keeping the `aria-describedby` attribute on the anchor even after the tooltip unmounted, causing screen readers to reference a non-existent element. Added a cleanup effect tied to the tooltip's portal lifecycle.

internal-design-system.tagline: Dark mode and reusable components for a shared design system
internal-design-system.description: Joined an existing design-system team to ship a dark-mode token layer and migrate 30+ components from class-based to functional patterns.
internal-design-system.impact: Enabled dark mode across 4 product surfaces in a single release, zero regression on existing consumers.
internal-design-system.technicalNotes:
## Token layer

The existing system used hardcoded hex values scattered across component files. Introduced a semantic token layer with `data-theme` attribute switching — light/dark themes are swapped without JavaScript by toggling a single attribute on `<html>`.

## Migration strategy

Class-based components were migrated incrementally using a codemods-first approach. Wrote a custom AST transform with `jscodeshift` to automate the boilerplate conversion, then manually reviewed each component's lifecycle methods.

cartographer.description: Interactive data-viz toolkit for geospatial dashboards — exploring D3 + WebGL rendering boundaries.
findings: WebGL canvas outperforms SVG by 10× at 50k+ data points
D3's projection math can be offloaded to a Web Worker without visual delay
Mapbox GL's custom layer API is sufficient for most data-viz overlays
cartographer.technicalNotes:
## Goal

Determine the practical rendering ceiling for browser-based geospatial dashboards and identify the best D3/WebGL integration point.

## Approach

Built a series of progressively complex visualizations — choropleth → point cloud → animated flow lines — and profiled each in Chrome DevTools. Compared SVG, Canvas 2D, and WebGL rendering for each case.

## Conclusion

For dashboards with < 5k features, SVG + D3 is the right choice (easy debugging, accessibility). Beyond that, Canvas 2D or WebGL is necessary. The `deck.gl` + Mapbox combination offers the best ergonomics for production use.

inbox-zero.description: Prototype AI email triage assistant with smart summarization using function-calling pipelines.
findings: Function-calling pipelines outperform prompt-only classification for structured extraction
Edge streaming cuts perceived latency by ~50% vs. waiting for full response
GPT-4o-mini is cost-effective enough for per-email processing at scale
inbox-zero.technicalNotes:
## Pipeline design

Each email passes through a 3-step function-calling pipeline:
1. **Classify** — label (action/info/promo/spam) + urgency score
2. **Summarize** — extract subject, sender intent, and required action
3. **Draft** — optional one-click reply draft

All steps run on Vercel Edge Functions with streaming so the UI updates progressively.

## Cost analysis

At GPT-4o-mini pricing, processing 100 emails/day costs ~$0.02. Acceptable for personal use; production would need batching + caching for repeated senders.

ledger-cli.description: A fast, scriptable command-line tool for plain-text accounting. Study in Go CLI design patterns.
findings: Go's stdlib is sufficient for most CLI tooling — cobra adds ergonomics, not capability
SQLite with WAL mode handles concurrent reads with zero configuration
Plain-text ledger format (hledger-compatible) is surprisingly robust for parsing
ledger-cli.technicalNotes:
## Motivation

Studied Go CLI architecture patterns by building a real tool I actually use — a plain-text accounting CLI compatible with the hledger format.

## Design decisions

- **cobra** for command routing and flag parsing
- **SQLite** (via `modernc.org/sqlite`) for the internal index — no CGo dependency
- **bubbletea** for the interactive TUI report viewer

## Learnings

Go's approach to CLI tooling is refreshingly pragmatic. The biggest lesson was around error handling — Go forces you to handle errors explicitly, which results in much more resilient CLI tools than equivalent Node.js scripts.

react-server-components.description: Hands-on exploration of RSC architecture: streaming, Suspense boundaries, and partial hydration tradeoffs.
findings: RSC eliminates client-side data-fetching waterfalls for deeply nested component trees
Suspense boundaries are the key unit of streaming — placement matters more than quantity
The RSC payload format is compact but adds non-trivial complexity to the build pipeline
Partial hydration via `use client` boundaries is the most impactful performance lever
react-server-components.technicalNotes:
## Scope

Built a series of increasingly complex Next.js App Router demos to stress-test RSC boundaries, streaming behavior, and the interop between server and client components.

## Key experiments

**Experiment 1 — Streaming waterfall elimination**: Replaced a deeply nested component tree that had 4 sequential `useEffect` fetches with RSC `async/await`. Result: 0 client-side waterfalls, ~40% reduction in TTI.

**Experiment 2 — Suspense placement**: Tested 3 different Suspense boundary configurations for the same UI. Found that coarse-grained boundaries (one per route segment) outperform fine-grained ones in practice because they reduce layout shifts.

**Experiment 3 — Client island size**: Measured JS bundle size as `use client` boundaries moved progressively closer to the leaves. Every level down reduced the hydrated JS by ~15–20%.

## Ongoing

Still exploring the cache invalidation model (`revalidatePath` vs `revalidateTag`) and its interaction with CDN-level caching.
